            "There absolutely was a market for gases in Faraday's time, but it was a very different kind of market from what we have today. And the distinction is fascinating: **Faraday was working at a time when gases were simultaneously scientific specimens, industrial commodities, and products that chemists often had to manufacture for themselves.**\n\nHe wasn't operating in a world where you could order a cylinder of pure nitrogen, oxygen, or carbon dioxide from an industrial gas supplier and have it delivered the next morning.\n\nIn the early 19th century, the gas trade was emerging, but it was fragmented. There were chemical manufacturers, pharmaceutical suppliers, instrument makers, mining operations, and a small but growing network of scientific institutions and private laboratories.\n\nFaraday occupied an interesting position right at the intersection of those worlds.\n\n## 1. What could Faraday actually buy?\n\nThere were several overlapping markets.\n\n| Market | What was available |\n|---|---|\n| Chemical manufacturers | Acids, salts, alkalis, minerals, chemical reagents |\n| Apothecaries and chemical dealers | Laboratory chemicals, prepared compounds, medicinal substances |\n| Gas-lighting companies | Manufactured illuminating gas, supplied through pipes or portable containers |\n| Instrument makers | Glassware, retorts, pumps, pressure apparatus |\n| Scientific networks | Samples, unusual substances, experimental materials exchanged between chemists |\n\nThe chemical trade was quite established. London's Society of Apothecaries, for example, had operated a substantial chemical manufacturing laboratory since 1672. By Faraday's time, commercial chemical production was an established industry. <Cite refs={[\"turn580705search4\",\"turn580705search11\",\"turn580705search6\"]}/>\n\nBut there was an important distinction:\n\n**Buying a chemical capable of producing a gas was considerably easier than buying the gas itself.**\n\n## 2. Faraday often manufactured his gases inside his apparatus\n\nThis is probably the most interesting part of your question.\n\nIn his original 1823 experiments, Faraday frequently didn't obtain a cylinder of gas. Instead, he obtained the ingredients needed to generate it.\n\nHe developed an ingenious technique using bent glass tubes, with the ingredients for producing a gas placed at one end.\n\n<AsyncImage query=\"Michael Faraday 1823 liquefaction of gases bent sealed glass tube original apparatus scientific illustration\" aspectRatio=\"5:4\" width=\"100%\" shop_eligible={false}/>\n\nThe procedure was approximately:\n\n1. Place the necessary chemical reactants in one end of a bent glass tube.\n2. Seal the tube.\n3. Heat the reactants to produce the gas.\n4. Allow the gas to accumulate pressure inside the sealed apparatus.\n5. Cool the opposite end, sometimes using ice or a freezing mixture.\n6. Observe whether the gas condensed into a liquid.\n\nHe was effectively creating his own miniature chemical production plant, pressure vessel, and refrigeration experiment in one piece of glassware.\n\nThe 1823 publication records nine gases successfully liquefied using this general approach. <Cite refs={[\"turn725213search0\",\"turn580705search13\"]}/>\n\nHis work included:\n\n- Chlorine\n- Hydrochloric acid (muriatic acid)\n- Sulphurous acid (sulfur dioxide)\n- Sulphuretted hydrogen (hydrogen sulfide)\n- Carbonic acid (carbon dioxide)\n- Nitrous oxide\n- Ammonia\n- Cyanogen\n- Euchlorine\n\nThere is a particularly interesting historical detail: Faraday's initial discovery of liquid chlorine emerged from investigating chlorine hydrate, rather than beginning with a commercially supplied sample of pure chlorine. Humphry Davy suggested heating the substance in a sealed tube. <Cite refs={[\"turn725213search11\",\"turn725213search9\"]}/>\n\n## 3. But there actually WAS a commercial gas business\n\nHere's where things get particularly interesting.\n\nLondon already had a developing commercial gas industry.\n\nThe gas-lighting revolution had begun, and companies were manufacturing gas by heating coal or other organic materials.\n\nOne particularly relevant example is the **London Portable Gas Company**, established in 1819.\n\nIt compressed gas produced from heating whale oil into copper cylinders at approximately 30 atmospheres.\n\nThese cylinders were supplied to wealthy households for illumination, particularly in places without access to piped gas.\n\nFaraday actually investigated the liquid residue accumulating in these cylinders. He separated and identified a previously unknown substance that became known as benzene. <Cite refs={[\"turn580705search0\",\"turn580705search7\"]}/>\n\n<AsyncImage query=\"early nineteenth century portable gas lighting copper gas cylinder whale oil historical illustration\" aspectRatio=\"16:9\" width=\"100%\" shop_eligible={false}/>\n\nSo Faraday wasn't entirely outside the commercial gas economy. He was investigating its products, too.\n\nHowever, manufactured illuminating gas was a mixture of compounds, not a convenient supply of individually purified gases.\n\n## 4. Did Faraday have to isolate everything himself?\n\nNo. And this distinction matters.\n\nThere were three different levels of acquisition:\n\n| What Faraday needed | How he could obtain it |\n|---|---|\n| Ordinary chemical ingredients | Purchase from chemical manufacturers |\n| Unusual compounds or gases | Prepare them himself or obtain samples through scientific contacts |\n| Pure gas for experimental work | Generate, purify, dry and collect it himself when necessary |\n\nFaraday also had access to the resources and scientific network of the Royal Institution, where he had worked since 1813. He wasn't an isolated amateur chemist trying to assemble an entire laboratory from scratch. <Cite refs={[\"turn725213search3\",\"turn580705search2\"]}/>\n\nHis correspondence even records him reporting successful experiments to colleagues and describing the gases he had obtained. <Cite refs={[\"turn725213search9\"]}/>\n\n## 5. An interesting consequence: the gas industry and cryogenics developed together\n\nThere is a historical progression worth noticing:\n\n- **1810s–1820s:** Commercial gas lighting develops. Chemical manufacturing expands.\n- **1823:** Faraday demonstrates that several supposedly permanent gases can be liquefied.\n- **1840s:** Faraday revisits liquefaction with substantially improved pressure and cooling techniques.\n- **1877:** Cailletet and Pictet achieve major breakthroughs in liquefying the so-called permanent gases, including oxygen.\n\n<Cite refs={[\"turn580705search0\",\"turn725213search1\",\"turn725213search33\"]}/>\n\nThe interesting thing is that the scientific problem wasn't simply obtaining gases. It was developing the infrastructure and techniques to manipulate them.\n\n---\n\n## One question this raises\n\nI think there's a potentially important distinction here, particularly if you're thinking about how experimental science operated in Faraday's era:\n\n**Faraday's laboratory was not primarily a place where he received finished scientific materials. It was a place where he manufactured the conditions and materials necessary to investigate nature.**\n\nThe boundary between chemical manufacturing, instrument engineering, and scientific experimentation was considerably less rigid than it is today.\n\nAnd that makes his work with gases especially interesting: he was investigating the physical properties of substances while simultaneously developing the means to produce, contain, purify, pressurize, cool, and observe them.\n\nIn a sense, he had to invent parts of the supply chain before he could conduct the experiment."

            "fallbackMarkdown": "There absolutely was a market for gases in Faraday's time, but it was a very different kind of market from what we have today. And the distinction is fascinating: **Faraday was working at a time when gases were simultaneously scientific specimens, industrial commodities, and products that chemists often had to manufacture for themselves.**\n\nHe wasn't operating in a world where you could order a cylinder of pure nitrogen, oxygen, or carbon dioxide from an industrial gas supplier and have it delivered the next morning.\n\nIn the early 19th century, the gas trade was emerging, but it was fragmented. There were chemical manufacturers, pharmaceutical suppliers, instrument makers, mining operations, and a small but growing network of scientific institutions and private laboratories.\n\nFaraday occupied an interesting position right at the intersection of those worlds.\n\n## 1\\. What could Faraday actually buy?\n\nThere were several overlapping markets.\n\n| Market | What was available |\n|--------|--------|\n| Chemical manufacturers | Acids, salts, alkalis, minerals, chemical reagents |\n| Apothecaries and chemical dealers | Laboratory chemicals, prepared compounds, medicinal substances |\n| Gas-lighting companies | Manufactured illuminating gas, supplied through pipes or portable containers |\n| Instrument makers | Glassware, retorts, pumps, pressure apparatus |\n| Scientific networks | Samples, unusual substances, experimental materials exchanged between chemists |\n\nThe chemical trade was quite established. London's Society of Apothecaries, for example, had operated a substantial chemical manufacturing laboratory since 1672. By Faraday's time, commercial chemical production was an established industry. citeturn580705search4turn580705search11turn580705search6\n\nBut there was an important distinction\\:\n\n**Buying a chemical capable of producing a gas was considerably easier than buying the gas itself.**\n\n## 2\\. Faraday often manufactured his gases inside his apparatus\n\nThis is probably the most interesting part of your question.\n\nIn his original 1823 experiments, Faraday frequently didn't obtain a cylinder of gas. Instead, he obtained the ingredients needed to generate it.\n\nHe developed an ingenious technique using bent glass tubes, with the ingredients for producing a gas placed at one end.\n\nimage_group{\"query\":[\"Michael Faraday 1823 liquefaction of gases bent sealed glass tube original apparatus scientific illustration\"],\"aspect_ratio\":\"5:4\",\"layout\":\"carousel\",\"num_per_query\":1}\n\nThe procedure was approximately\\:\n\n1. Place the necessary chemical reactants in one end of a bent glass tube.\n2. Seal the tube.\n3. Heat the reactants to produce the gas.\n4. Allow the gas to accumulate pressure inside the sealed apparatus.\n5. Cool the opposite end, sometimes using ice or a freezing mixture.\n6. Observe whether the gas condensed into a liquid.\n\nHe was effectively creating his own miniature chemical production plant, pressure vessel, and refrigeration experiment in one piece of glassware.\n\nThe 1823 publication records nine gases successfully liquefied using this general approach. citeturn725213search0turn580705search13\n\nHis work included\\:\n\n- Chlorine\n- Hydrochloric acid (muriatic acid)\n- Sulphurous acid (sulfur dioxide)\n- Sulphuretted hydrogen (hydrogen sulfide)\n- Carbonic acid (carbon dioxide)\n- Nitrous oxide\n- Ammonia\n- Cyanogen\n- Euchlorine\n\nThere is a particularly interesting historical detail: Faraday's initial discovery of liquid chlorine emerged from investigating chlorine hydrate, rather than beginning with a commercially supplied sample of pure chlorine. Humphry Davy suggested heating the substance in a sealed tube. citeturn725213search11turn725213search9\n\n## 3\\. But there actually WAS a commercial gas business\n\nHere's where things get particularly interesting.\n\nLondon already had a developing commercial gas industry.\n\nThe gas-lighting revolution had begun, and companies were manufacturing gas by heating coal or other organic materials.\n\nOne particularly relevant example is the **London Portable Gas Company**, established in 1819.\n\nIt compressed gas produced from heating whale oil into copper cylinders at approximately 30 atmospheres.\n\nThese cylinders were supplied to wealthy households for illumination, particularly in places without access to piped gas.\n\nFaraday actually investigated the liquid residue accumulating in these cylinders. He separated and identified a previously unknown substance that became known as benzene. citeturn580705search0turn580705search7\n\nimage_group{\"query\":[\"early nineteenth century portable gas lighting copper gas cylinder whale oil historical illustration\"],\"aspect_ratio\":\"16:9\",\"layout\":\"carousel\",\"num_per_query\":1}\n\nSo Faraday wasn't entirely outside the commercial gas economy. He was investigating its products, too.\n\nHowever, manufactured illuminating gas was a mixture of compounds, not a convenient supply of individually purified gases.\n\n## 4\\. Did Faraday have to isolate everything himself?\n\nNo. And this distinction matters.\n\nThere were three different levels of acquisition\\:\n\n| What Faraday needed | How he could obtain it |\n|--------|--------|\n| Ordinary chemical ingredients | Purchase from chemical manufacturers |\n| Unusual compounds or gases | Prepare them himself or obtain samples through scientific contacts |\n| Pure gas for experimental work | Generate, purify, dry and collect it himself when necessary |\n\nFaraday also had access to the resources and scientific network of the Royal Institution, where he had worked since 1813. He wasn't an isolated amateur chemist trying to assemble an entire laboratory from scratch. citeturn725213search3turn580705search2\n\nHis correspondence even records him reporting successful experiments to colleagues and describing the gases he had obtained. citeturn725213search9\n\n## 5\\. An interesting consequence: the gas industry and cryogenics developed together\n\nThere is a historical progression worth noticing\\:\n\n- **1810s–1820s\\:** Commercial gas lighting develops. Chemical manufacturing expands.\n- **1823\\:** Faraday demonstrates that several supposedly permanent gases can be liquefied.\n- **1840s\\:** Faraday revisits liquefaction with substantially improved pressure and cooling techniques.\n- **1877\\:** Cailletet and Pictet achieve major breakthroughs in liquefying the so-called permanent gases, including oxygen.\n\nciteturn580705search0turn725213search1turn725213search33\n\nThe interesting thing is that the scientific problem wasn't simply obtaining gases. It was developing the infrastructure and techniques to manipulate them.\n\n---\n\n## One question this raises\n\nI think there's a potentially important distinction here, particularly if you're thinking about how experimental science operated in Faraday's era\\:\n\n**Faraday's laboratory was not primarily a place where he received finished scientific materials. It was a place where he manufactured the conditions and materials necessary to investigate nature.**\n\nThe boundary between chemical manufacturing, instrument engineering, and scientific experimentation was considerably less rigid than it is today.\n\nAnd that makes his work with gases especially interesting: he was investigating the physical properties of substances while simultaneously developing the means to produce, contain, purify, pressurize, cool, and observe them.\n\nIn a sense, he had to invent parts of the supply chain before he could conduct the experiment.",

          "parts": [
            "Yes! **It was still predominantly in the gas phase.** But there is a fascinating wrinkle: the compression process was actually causing part of the gas mixture to liquefy.\n\nThe London Portable Gas Company was storing oil gas at approximately **30 atmospheres**, or about 30 times ordinary atmospheric pressure, in copper cylinders. The gas was manufactured from oil, including whale and other animal oils. <Cite refs={[\"turn377260search13\",\"turn377260search12\"]}/>\n\n<AsyncImage query=\"1819 London portable gas copper cylinder Gordon patent portable gas lamp historical illustration\" aspectRatio=\"16:9\" width=\"100%\" shop_eligible={false}/>\n\n## What was happening inside the cylinders?\n\nThink of the gas as a mixture of different hydrocarbons, each with its own boiling point and condensation behavior.\n\nWhen they compressed the mixture:\n\n1. The pressure increased enormously.\n2. Some of the heavier hydrocarbons condensed into liquid.\n3. The remaining mixture stayed gaseous under pressure.\n4. The liquid accumulated at the bottom of the receiving vessel.\n\nThis wasn't just a theoretical possibility. It is precisely what Faraday investigated in 1825.\n\nHe received samples of this liquid residue from David Gordon, associated with the Portable Gas Company.\n\nFaraday described how the gas passed from a gasometer into a large pressure receiver, where condensation occurred. The liquid could then be drawn off through a valve at the bottom.\n\n**And here's the remarkable part: this investigation led to the discovery of benzene.**\n\nFaraday estimated that 1,000 cubic feet of oil gas yielded nearly one gallon of the liquid. <Cite refs={[\"turn377260search0\",\"turn377260search14\"]}/>\n\n## So there were actually two different kinds of liquefaction happening\n\n| Process | What happened |\n|---|---|\n| Commercial gas compression | Certain components of a gas mixture condensed incidentally under pressure |\n| Faraday's experiments | Deliberately manipulating pressure and temperature to liquefy particular gases |\n\nThe distinction is important.\n\nThe gas company wasn't trying to liquefy its product. It wanted to store illuminating gas efficiently. The liquid was essentially a byproduct.\n\nFaraday recognized that this byproduct was scientifically valuable.\n\n## One more thing worth appreciating\n\nThe company was effectively operating an early compressed-gas distribution network:\n\n- Gas manufactured centrally.\n- Compressed into reusable copper vessels.\n- Delivered to customers.\n- Connected to specialized lamps.\n- Empty vessels collected and refilled.\n\nThat is recognizably an industrial gas supply chain, even though it predates the modern industrial gas industry by decades.\n\n**Faraday was essentially mining the unwanted liquid fraction of somebody else's industrial process for new chemistry.**\n\nThat's a rather wonderful example of industrial technology accidentally opening a door to fundamental science."

          "parts": [
            "The trick is that they didn't necessarily have to see through the copper cylinder. They could detect the liquid through the behavior of the apparatus and, more importantly, through the way the gas was transferred.\n\nThere are actually two separate vessels in this story, and that's an important distinction:\n\n1. The portable copper gas cylinders used to store and transport the compressed illuminating gas.\n2. The receiving apparatus into which the gas was transferred and where Faraday investigated the condensate.\n\nThe second is where the chemistry becomes visible.\n\nAnd we have Faraday's own description, which is even better than a reconstruction.\n\nIn his 1825 paper, *On New Compounds of Carbon and Hydrogen*, he explains:\n\n> \"It is in the receiver that the condensation principally takes place; and it is from that vessel that the liquid I have worked with has been taken.\"\n\nHe describes a conical valve at the bottom of the receiver. When opened:\n\n- Water came out first.\n- Then the oily liquid.\n- As it emerged, it effervesced.\n- A dense, transparent vapor could actually be seen descending from the outlet.\n- Once the liquid was collected, it could be stored in ordinary stoppered bottles, even corked ones.\n\n<Cite refs={[\"turn879506search18\",\"turn879506search0\"]}/>\n\n**So the really surprising answer is that the liquid wasn't discovered by inspecting the inside of a copper cylinder. The industrial apparatus was designed in such a way that the condensate could be drained off.**\n\nAnd there's a lovely industrial-science feedback loop here: the company noticed that its illuminating gas was losing brightness, while Faraday saw an opportunity to investigate the material responsible.\n\nThe residue that was commercially inconvenient became one of the most consequential discoveries in organic chemistry: benzene.\n\nYou can read Faraday's original paper here: <Link ref=\"turn879506search18\" title=\"On New Compounds of Carbon and Hydrogen (1825), original paper\"/>."

            "You're reconstructing the phase behavior correctly in broad strokes, but there's one important correction that makes the historical apparatus even more interesting:\n\n**The bulk of Faraday's benzene-containing condensate accumulated in the large stationary receiving vessel at the gasworks, BEFORE the gas was transferred into the portable copper cylinders.**\n\nFaraday explicitly says so in his 1825 paper. He describes gas passing from a gasometer over water into a large, strong receiver, then through pipes into the portable vessels. The liquid was drawn from the bottom of that receiver. <Cite refs={[\"turn596798search0\",\"turn596798search35\"]}/>\n\nThat also means I need to correct something from my earlier explanation: I made it sound as though the portable cylinders themselves were where the principal accumulation occurred. Faraday's account says otherwise.\n\n## 1. Your hydrocarbon condensation sequence\n\nYour intuition about preferential condensation is right. The heavier, less volatile hydrocarbons generally condense before the lighter ones as pressure increases or temperature decreases.\n\nA simplified ordering, from easiest to hardest to keep gaseous, is:\n\n| Compound | Normal boiling point |\n|---|---:|\n| Nonane | 150.8°C |\n| Octane | 125.6°C |\n| Heptane | 98.4°C |\n| Hexane | 68.7°C |\n| Benzene | 80.1°C |\n| Pentane | 36.1°C |\n| Butane | −0.5°C |\n| Propane | −42.1°C |\n| Ethane | −88.6°C |\n| Methane | −161.5°C |\n\nBenzene is an interesting exception to the ordering by carbon number: it boils above hexane.\n\nBut there are two important qualifications:\n\n- These are pure-substance boiling points, not the actual condensation sequence in a multicomponent gas mixture. Partial pressures and mixture composition matter.\n- Methane cannot be liquefied by pressure alone at ordinary room temperature. Its critical temperature is approximately −82.6°C. Above that temperature, no amount of pressure produces an ordinary liquid phase.\n\nSo yes, at sufficiently high pressure, propane and other heavier hydrocarbons could condense. Methane would require substantial cooling.\n\n## 2. The water is a separate story\n\nYou noticed something important when you mentioned the water dew point.\n\nFaraday says the gas was initially held in a gasometer **over water**. That means it could carry water vapor into the receiver.\n\nWhen compressed, the partial pressure of that water vapor increased. If it exceeded the saturation vapor pressure at the receiver's temperature, water condensed.\n\nFaraday actually describes the drainage sequence:\n\n1. Water emerged first.\n2. The hydrocarbon liquid followed.\n\nThat's a nice little piece of experimental evidence about the separation of the two liquid phases. <Cite refs={[\"turn596798search0\",\"turn596798search6\"]}/>\n\n## 3. And those pictures!\n\nYour instincts about the images are pretty good.\n\n- **First image:** I agree that it doesn't look like an ordinary gas cylinder. The lifting eye, rounded body and fittings suggest some kind of specialized pressure vessel, buoyant apparatus, or possibly ordnance. I wouldn't identify it without its provenance.\n- **Second image:** This is more plausibly a pressure vessel, but the flange and nozzle alone aren't enough to establish its purpose or date.\n- **Third image:** The horse-drawn vehicle with multiple interconnected cylindrical vessels looks like industrial gas transportation equipment. The arrangement is particularly interesting because the vessels appear to be individually connected to a common distribution manifold.\n- **Fourth image:** I wouldn't call that a tank with a person inside! The figure appears to be standing alongside the vehicle. It could be a specialized military or industrial transport apparatus, but the precise identification needs its original caption.\n\nThe third illustration is particularly worth investigating. It may be much closer to the later industrial gas-delivery system than to Faraday's original equipment.\n\n## 4. One historical correction to our mental picture\n\n<AsyncImage query=\"1819 David Gordon Edward Heard London Portable Gas Company copper portable gas cylinder historical patent illustration\" aspectRatio=\"16:9\" width=\"100%\" shop_eligible={false}/>\n\nThe original portable vessels weren't necessarily enormous, either.\n\nThe Historic England industrial history gives their capacities as approximately 1 to 5 cubic feet, with hemispherical ends. They were copper, operated at 30 atmospheres, and fitted with regulating valves. <Cite refs={[\"turn596798search35\",\"turn596798search2\"]}/>\n\nThat's a surprisingly compact technology.\n\nAnd here's the detail I'd really like to chase: the company had a *large stationary receiver* where much of the condensation happened, followed by smaller portable vessels.\n\nIn other words, **they had inadvertently created an early hydrocarbon fractionation opportunity, even though they weren't operating a refinery or deliberately separating hydrocarbons.**\n\nI think there's a very interesting history of industrial gas engineering hiding behind Faraday's famous experiment. The actual apparatus, its operating pressures, its valves, its gas composition and its condensate would make a wonderful reconstruction project."

            "Now you've got my attention. That is a wonderfully strange contraption. And I think your boiler observation is the most useful clue.\n\nI would put the possibilities in this order:\n\n## 1. A mobile steam-powered apparatus\n\n<badge color=\"success\">Leading hypothesis</badge>\n\nThe large cylindrical body, domed ends, apparent fittings and wheeled carriage are consistent with a portable boiler or pressure vessel.\n\nThere were plenty of experimental mobile steam apparatuses in the 19th century, including horse-drawn industrial equipment.\n\nThe Science Museum has an example of an early 19th-century *wagon boiler*, a cylindrical boiler designed for stationary and mobile steam applications. <Cite refs={[\"turn101361search6\"]}/>\n\n## 2. An incendiary projector\n\n<badge color=\"warning\">Interesting possibility</badge>\n\nBelieve it or not, your flamethrower suggestion isn't nearly as anachronistic as it sounds.\n\n- In 1702, the Prussian military tested an incendiary projector called the *Schlangen-Brand-Spritze* (serpent fire-spray).\n- In 1814, American inventor Uriah Brown demonstrated a steam-powered flamethrower.\n- In 1901, Richard Fiedler patented the modern German flamethrower concept.\n\n<Cite refs={[\"turn838153search0\",\"turn838153search1\",\"turn838153search39\"]}/>\n\nSo there is a genuine historical lineage of pressurized incendiary projectors.\n\nHowever, I'd expect an actual flame projector to have some recognizable fuel-delivery apparatus, such as a hose or directional lance. I can't confidently identify one in this engraving.\n\n## 3. A cannon or pneumatic weapon\n\nPossible, but I'm less convinced.\n\nA conventional cannon would have a recognizable barrel, breech and mounting arrangement. This looks much more like a pressure vessel with an outlet than a conventional artillery piece.\n\nA pneumatic or steam-powered projectile launcher is conceivable, but we'd need more evidence.\n\n## What I would investigate next\n\nThe engraving's original caption is probably the key. In particular, I'd look for the German terms:\n\n- *Dampfspritze*: steam-powered pump or fire engine.\n- *Dampfkanone*: steam cannon.\n- *Feuerspritze*: fire engine.\n- *Brand-Spritze*: incendiary projector.\n- *Dampfapparat*: steam apparatus.\n\nOne question: **Where did you find the illustration, and what was the exact Prussian identification attached to it?**\n\nEven a partial caption or the name of the publication could help us identify the machine. I don't want to turn an obscure piece of 19th-century engineering into a flamethrower merely because it looks like something designed by an unusually aggressive plumber."

            "There it is! And the caption answers almost everything. Your transcription is very close. The ambiguous letter is almost certainly an **L**, giving us:\n\n**Panzerlafette für eine 5,3-Centimeter-Schnellfeuerkanone L/24, aufgeprotzt.**\n\nTranslation:\n\n*Armored gun carriage for a 5.3-centimeter quick-firing cannon, barrel length 24 calibers, limbered for transport.*\n\nThere are three particularly interesting bits of terminology here.\n\n- **Panzerlafette:** Armored gun mounting or carriage. *Lafette* is the gun's supporting and aiming structure.\n- **Schnellfeuerkanone:** Quick-firing cannon.\n- **Aufgeprotzt:** Connected to its *Protze*, the small two-wheeled limber used to hitch an artillery piece to its horses for transportation.\n\nThat last word is the giveaway!\n\n## And now the horses make perfect sense\n\nA conventional artillery piece was transported with its barrel pointing backward, attached to the limber in front.\n\n<AsyncImage query=\"19th century German horse drawn artillery gun limber Protze historical engraving\" aspectRatio=\"16:9\" width=\"100%\" shop_eligible={false}/>\n\nThe procedure was:\n\n1. The gun carriage was attached to the limber.\n2. Horses pulled the combined assembly.\n3. At the destination, the gun was unlimbered.\n4. The gun was positioned, aimed and fired.\n5. It was limbered again for movement.\n\nSo the horse-drawn contraption isn't a self-propelled armored vehicle. It's an armored artillery piece in its transportation configuration.\n\n## A further historical discovery\n\nI found an 1890 German newspaper account describing trials of a 5.3 cm quick-firing cannon in a mobile armored carriage.\n\nIt reports:\n- Nine shots at 1,500 metres with horses attached.\n- Deployment into a firing position within 17 minutes.\n- Another trial involving ten rapid-fire shots at 1,200 metres.\n- The gun was subsequently limbered up again.\n\n<Cite refs={[\"turn811932search1\"]}/>\n\nAnd there's a related identification in the 1893 *Brockhaus Konversations-Lexikon*: \n\n**Gruson's 5.3 cm Schnellfeuerkanone L/25 in Schumann's mobile armored carriage.**\n\nThat is very close to your L/24 caption, although the one-caliber discrepancy means we shouldn't assume they're precisely the same gun configuration.\n\nSo we have a much better identification now: **a late-19th-century German armored quick-firing artillery carriage, associated with the Gruson/Schumann system.**\n\nAnd I owe you a correction: my earlier confident identification as a Fahrpanzer was too specific.           "parts": [
            "Yes! That's the wonderfully peculiar implication of the design. The gun carriage wasn't merely transporting a cannon. **The armored enclosure was intended to protect the gun crew while operating the weapon.**\n\nBut there's one detail I'd separate: the soldier shown handling the horses isn't necessarily the man who operated the gun. The engraving may be showing the transport crew, rather than the complete firing procedure.\n\nThe likely sequence was:\n\n1. Tow the armored gun into position.\n2. Unlimber it from the horse-drawn transport arrangement.\n3. Move the horses and driver away from the firing position.\n4. Get the gun crew into the armored mounting.\n5. Operate the gun through its protected firing aperture.\n\nAnd we can do better than infer this from the picture. Hermann Gruson's 1887 patent, US 367,617, actually describes the arrangement in detail.\n\n<AsyncImage query=\"Hermann Gruson 1887 patent 367617 gun carriage sectional drawing gunner inside armored casing\" aspectRatio=\"5:4\" width=\"100%\" shop_eligible={false}/>\n\nThe patent specifies:\n\n- An armored casing with an actual **entrance door**.\n- A platform or floor inside.\n- A rotating armored dome with the gun barrel projecting through an aperture.\n- A seat for the gunner.\n- Controls allowing him to traverse the gun by pushing against the floor with his feet and against a support with his shoulder.\n- Hand controls for elevation and depression.\n\nGruson explicitly says the arrangement protects the gunner while allowing him to operate the weapon. <Cite refs={[\"turn786269view0\"]}/>\n\nSo your mental reconstruction is substantially correct, with one adjustment:\n\n**The driver and gunner were separate jobs.** The driver handled the horses and transport. The gunner entered the armored enclosure once the weapon was deployed.\n\nAnd the really extraordinary part? The gunner could rotate the armored dome and traverse the gun while remaining inside his little steel room.\n\nImagine being the poor infantryman approaching what looks like a squat iron barrel on wheels, and discovering that there's a fellow inside actively aiming it at you.\n\nNineteenth-century military engineering had some wonderfully peculiar ideas."

            "You caught a real ambiguity, and I think your objection is justified. I went back to Gruson's actual 1887 patent, and it contains a rather delightful clarification.\n\n**The gunner was inside. There was also a second man, but he wasn't another gunner.**\n\nGruson explicitly writes that one man operates the gun, while another supplies ammunition, sitting at the entrance to the casing. The ammunition boxes hang from a rail inside the enclosure, within the gunner's reach. <Cite refs={[\"turn730115search0\",\"turn730115search22\"]}/>\n\nSo the patent describes a two-man operating arrangement, despite having only one actual gunner.\n\nBut here's the twist: Gruson's patent says the second man sits at the entrance, supplying ammunition. He isn't necessarily the horse driver. <Cite refs={[\"turn306361view0\"]}/>\n\nSo we have three functions to account for:\n\n- **Gunner:** Inside the armored turret, seated at the controls.\n- **Ammunition attendant:** At the entrance, feeding cartridges into the supply rail.\n- **Transport attendant:** Handling the horses and towing arrangement.\n\nThe engraving shows only one visible person. We cannot establish from that image alone whether the gunner is already inside during transport, whether the ammunition attendant is omitted, or whether the illustration depicts a simplified transport arrangement.\n\nAnd I particularly like your alternative explanation:\n\n*Or he's the one engraving the image.*\n\nA remarkably secure occupation, provided the enemy doesn't notice the artist."

            "That's a wonderfully plausible counterfactual. The history of chemistry might have hinged on where somebody put a drain valve.\n\nBut there's a slight complication: **the liquid wasn't necessarily hidden from everyone until Faraday came along.** The gasworks operators had noticed problems with their illuminating gas, including loss of illuminating power and accumulation of liquid residues.\n\nThe distinction is that they regarded the condensate as an operational nuisance, whereas Faraday recognized it as an experimental specimen.\n\nAnd your top-mounted outlet scenario is interesting:\n\n- With a bottom outlet, condensed liquid could be deliberately drained and collected.\n- With a top outlet, the gas could leave while the liquid remained behind.\n- If the vessel were moved, somebody might hear or feel liquid sloshing.\n- If the vessel were stationary, they might simply notice reduced usable capacity or changing gas behavior.\n\nBut they wouldn't necessarily have avoided the liquid. They might have drained it during maintenance, discarded it, or attributed it to contamination.\n\n**The really consequential accident wasn't the condensation itself. It was someone deciding that the stuff coming out of the bottom deserved to be investigated.**\n\nFaraday had a particular advantage here: he was already interested in the question of whether supposedly permanent gases could be liquefied. The gasworks had inadvertently produced exactly the kind of material he wanted to study.\n\nA beautiful example of scientific curiosity finding value in somebody else's industrial waste."

            "Now there's an amusing correction to our picture of the Georgian country gentleman: **No, he probably wasn't boiling whale oil in the scullery to manufacture his own illuminating gas.** I may have accidentally invented a rather unpleasant domestic industry!\n\nThere were actually two different technologies involved.\n\n### 1. The traditional whale-oil lamp\n\n<AsyncImage query=\"Georgian Regency period whale oil Argand oil lamp brass glass chimney antique\" aspectRatio=\"5:4\" shop_eligible={true}/>\n\nWhale oil was sold as a finished liquid fuel. The household simply filled its lamps and burned it directly.\n\nSperm-whale oil was particularly prized because it burned relatively cleanly and brightly. <Cite refs={[\"turn192199search0\",\"turn192199search4\"]}/>\n\n### 2. Manufactured illuminating gas\n\n<AsyncImage query=\"early nineteenth century oil gas retort apparatus historical engraving\" aspectRatio=\"5:4\" shop_eligible={false}/>\n\nThis involved heating a feedstock in an enclosed retort to produce combustible gas.\n\nCoal was the dominant feedstock in the developing gas industry, but oil could also be used. The gas was manufactured commercially, rather than by householders boiling lamp oil. <Cite refs={[\"turn192199search1\",\"turn192199search23\"]}/>\n\n### 3. What was the country gentleman actually doing in 1819?\n\nProbably still using:\n- Whale-oil lamps.\n- Vegetable-oil lamps.\n- Candles, including expensive beeswax candles.\n- Oil lamps with improved Argand burners.\n\nPrivate gasworks existed, but were initially concentrated around factories and mills. Gas lighting in wealthy private homes became more established during the 1840s. <Cite refs={[\"turn192199search1\",\"turn192199search22\"]}/>\n\n**The portable oil-gas service was offering something genuinely new:** the convenience of manufactured illuminating gas without requiring the customer to build and operate a gasworks.\n\nSo our imaginary advertisement needs a slight rewrite:\n\n*Gentlemen! Tired of tending your lamps? Bring the latest industrial marvel to your country estate! No retorts, no gasworks, no troublesome manufacturing. Just connect your portable gas vessel and illuminate!*\n\nThe whale, meanwhile, was already dead. No further boiling required."

            "The advantage was primarily **more light, lower operating cost, and less domestic maintenance**. But there's a distinction worth making: they weren't compressing whale oil. They were converting it into illuminating gas by heating it in a closed retort, then compressing the resulting gas for delivery.\n\nAnd I think by \"liquid whale-head extraction\" you mean spermaceti or sperm oil, which came from the head of the sperm whale. That's a different product from ordinary whale oil rendered from blubber.\n\nThe two technologies were competing ways of getting useful illumination out of the same animal.\n\n## 1. The comparison: burning oil versus burning gas\n\n- **Sperm oil:** Refined liquid fuel burned directly in a lamp with a wick.\n- **Oil gas:** Oil thermally decomposed in a retort, producing combustible gases that were collected, compressed and burned through a gas burner.\n\nThe second process was effectively converting a liquid fuel into a transportable gaseous fuel.\n\n## 2. The economics were surprisingly compelling\n\nHere's a contemporary comparison published in Frederick Accum's 1819 *Description of the Process of Manufacturing Coal Gas*, drawing on figures supplied by the Taylors.\n\n| Lighting method | Cost per hour |\n|---|---:|\n| Oil-gas Argand burner | ¾ penny |\n| Two sperm-oil Argand lamps | 3 pence |\n| Ten tallow candles | 3½ pence |\n| Wax candles | 14 pence |\n\nThe oil-gas burner reportedly produced illumination equivalent to two Argand lamps, or ten mould candles. <Cite refs={[\"turn796897search4\",\"turn796897search6\"]}/>\n\n<badge color=\"success\">About 75% cheaper</badge>\n\nCompared with the two sperm-oil lamps, the published estimate put oil gas at one-quarter the operating cost.\n\nThat's a substantial difference, although these are contemporary promotional economics, not a modern independently controlled comparison.\n\n## 3. Why gas was attractive beyond the price\n\n| Advantage | Oil lamp | Portable oil gas |\n|---|---|---|\n| Fuel handling | Fill individual lamps | Exchange gas vessels |\n| Maintenance | Trim wicks, clean reservoirs and chimneys | Maintain burners and connections |\n| Light distribution | Limited by lamp placement | Small gas pipes and movable lamps |\n| Illumination | Good, but dependent on burner | Bright, consistent flame |\n| Fuel efficiency | Direct combustion | More efficient light production according to contemporary estimates |\n| Domestic convenience | Regular attention | Much less attention |\n\nThe London Portable Gas Company added another clever feature: customers received replacement vessels daily, so they weren't expected to manage their own gas production or refill equipment. <Cite refs={[\"turn796897search12\"]}/>\n\n## 4. But what about spermaceti?\n\n<AsyncImage query=\"19th century spermaceti candle whale head spermaceti oil historical illustration\" aspectRatio=\"16:9\" shop_eligible={false}/>\n\nSpermaceti was particularly valuable for candles and specialized lighting. It produced a relatively clean, bright flame.\n\nHowever, the oil-gas process could extract useful illuminating energy from ordinary whale oil, including less valuable grades. The 1819 account specifically notes that cheaper oils could work nearly as well.\n\nThat potentially changed the economics of the entire whaling industry: rather than reserving the best oils for illumination, manufacturers could turn lower-cost feedstock into a competitive lighting fuel. <Cite refs={[\"turn796897search4\",\"turn796897search15\"]}/>\n\n**The really interesting distinction:** Spermaceti lamps were an improvement in the quality of traditional lighting. Oil gas was an attempt to replace the entire lighting system.\n\nAnd that was the bigger revolution. You weren't buying a better lamp. You were buying into a new energy-distribution system, complete with fuel production, compression, delivery, storage and standardized burners.\n\nFaraday's benzene was an accidental dividend from that industrial transformation."

            "fallbackMarkdown": "The advantage was primarily **more light, lower operating cost, and less domestic maintenance**\\. But there's a distinction worth making: they weren't compressing whale oil. They were converting it into illuminating gas by heating it in a closed retort, then compressing the resulting gas for delivery.\n\nAnd I think by \"liquid whale-head extraction\" you mean spermaceti or sperm oil, which came from the head of the sperm whale. That's a different product from ordinary whale oil rendered from blubber.\n\nThe two technologies were competing ways of getting useful illumination out of the same animal.\n\n## 1\\. The comparison: burning oil versus burning gas\n\n- **Sperm oil\\:** Refined liquid fuel burned directly in a lamp with a wick.\n- **Oil gas\\:** Oil thermally decomposed in a retort, producing combustible gases that were collected, compressed and burned through a gas burner.\n\nThe second process was effectively converting a liquid fuel into a transportable gaseous fuel.\n\n## 2\\. The economics were surprisingly compelling\n\nHere's a contemporary comparison published in Frederick Accum's 1819 *Description of the Process of Manufacturing Coal Gas*, drawing on figures supplied by the Taylors.\n\n| Lighting method | Cost per hour |\n|--------|--------|\n| Oil-gas Argand burner | ¾ penny |\n| Two sperm-oil Argand lamps | 3 pence |\n| Ten tallow candles | 3½ pence |\n| Wax candles | 14 pence |\n\nThe oil-gas burner reportedly produced illumination equivalent to two Argand lamps, or ten mould candles. citeturn796897search4turn796897search6\n\n(About 75% cheaper)\n\nCompared with the two sperm-oil lamps, the published estimate put oil gas at one-quarter the operating cost.\n\nThat's a substantial difference, although these are contemporary promotional economics, not a modern independently controlled comparison.\n\n## 3\\. Why gas was attractive beyond the price\n\n| Advantage | Oil lamp | Portable oil gas |\n|--------|--------|--------|\n| Fuel handling | Fill individual lamps | Exchange gas vessels |\n| Maintenance | Trim wicks, clean reservoirs and chimneys | Maintain burners and connections |\n| Light distribution | Limited by lamp placement | Small gas pipes and movable lamps |\n| Illumination | Good, but dependent on burner | Bright, consistent flame |\n| Fuel efficiency | Direct combustion | More efficient light production according to contemporary estimates |\n| Domestic convenience | Regular attention | Much less attention |\n\nThe London Portable Gas Company added another clever feature: customers received replacement vessels daily, so they weren't expected to manage their own gas production or refill equipment. citeturn796897search12\n\n## 4\\. But what about spermaceti?\nimage_group{\"query\":[\"19th century spermaceti candle whale head spermaceti oil historical illustration\"],\"aspect_ratio\":\"16:9\",\"layout\":\"carousel\",\"num_per_query\":1}\n\nSpermaceti was particularly valuable for candles and specialized lighting. It produced a relatively clean, bright flame.\n\nHowever, the oil-gas process could extract useful illuminating energy from ordinary whale oil, including less valuable grades. The 1819 account specifically notes that cheaper oils could work nearly as well.\n\nThat potentially changed the economics of the entire whaling industry: rather than reserving the best oils for illumination, manufacturers could turn lower-cost feedstock into a competitive lighting fuel. citeturn796897search4turn796897search15\n\n**The really interesting distinction\\:** Spermaceti lamps were an improvement in the quality of traditional lighting. Oil gas was an attempt to replace the entire lighting system.\n\nAnd that was the bigger revolution. You weren't buying a better lamp.             "A **cheroot** is indeed a type of cigar, and a wonderfully Dickensian word. You've probably encountered it in a period novel, an old Western, or a description of some disreputable gentleman leaning against a tavern door.\n\n<AsyncImageGroup query={[\"cheroot cigar unwrapped tobacco cigar\",\"Victorian gentleman smoking cheroot historical illustration\"]} aspectRatio=\"5:4\" layout=\"carousel\" shop_eligible={false}/>\n\nA few distinctions:\n\n- **Cheroot:** A short, usually cylindrical cigar, traditionally open at both ends. Unlike a conventional cigar, it often has no tapered, closed head. The name comes from the Tamil *curuttu*, meaning roll.\n- **Cigar:** Usually wrapped in tobacco leaf, with one end closed and rounded or tapered, the other cut for smoking.\n- **Cigarillo:** A small, thin cigar, generally more modern in its commercial form.\n- **Cigarette:** Finely cut tobacco rolled in paper.\n\nCheroots were particularly associated with India and Southeast Asia, and became familiar to British smokers through colonial trade. They were often depicted as the smoking accessory of military men, merchants, and adventurers.\n\nAnd regarding the industrial workforce: I withdraw the lemonade-stand comparison.
